extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science/public administration; readers studying party systems, political leadership, and accountability
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the role, power, and accountability of party leaders ('bosses') and the institutional features that make government popular or responsible. Focuses on comparative mechanisms (American vs. parliamentary systems) that enable or limit removal and responsibility of party leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's power to force an unpopular party out of control
rubrics_metrics.description: "What the people should have, if the government is to be really popular in character, is the power at a given time to force an unpopular party out of the control of the government, and to oblige the party leaders in whom they do not have confidence to lay down their rights of leadership, giving place to others more in accord with the public will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts this as a core test of a truly popular government: until the electorate can effect this change in party control and leadership, the government cannot be regarded as popular. This frames evaluation of systems by the ease with which the public can remove a controlling party and its leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of retirement from control of public affairs of a party that has lost confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The American political system "does not in the first place permit the easy retirement, from the control of public affairs, of a party which has lost the confidence of the people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to judge whether institutional design allows a ruling party that has lost popular confidence to cede power readily (e.g., mechanisms for turnover, electoral responsiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Party members' internal power to change party leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The system "does not... give the party members, in case they disapprove of policies proposed by party leaders, the power to bring about as easily as is desirable a change in party leadership."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess internal party rules and customs (primaries, conventions, recall of leaders) that let rank-and-file members replace leaders without undue friction or external coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electorate's effective choice vs mere candidate selection
rubrics_metrics.description: "The power the people practically have at an election is merely to choose between several candidates, none of whom they may desire, and who, if elected, do not have the power always to secure the adoption of the popular policy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether elections give voters realistic ability to enact popular policy or merely provide selection among preexisting elites; consider candidate selection processes, party control of nominations, and alignment of elected officials with popular preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party organization as the point of attack for preserving popular government
rubrics_metrics.description: "The point of attack by those who believe in the preservation of popular government is not so much the formal governmental system as the party organization."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing failures of popular government, examine party structures (primaries, nomination rules, intra-party democracy) and reforms aimed at them rather than only formal governmental institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of party control in a single person (the boss) undermines popular government
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties "have fallen or are falling under the control of a single person" — a tendency regarded "as an extremely unfortunate one, and as presaging the destruction of popular government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the degree to which single individuals dominate party organization and decision-making; high concentration is treated as a negative indicator for popular government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which the boss controls making and enforcement of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: "They control the making of laws and their execution after they are made."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the de facto power of party leaders over legislative and administrative outcomes (through nominations, party discipline, patronage), even if formal institutions appear pluralistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility/accountability of political leadership (power with responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Power without responsibility is a thing against which the human race has been fighting since its first attempts at political organization."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether holders of concentrated political power can be held accountable (by voters, legislature, or other institutions). The absence of accountability is a serious normative failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of fixing responsibility in systems with diffuse constitutional checks and decentralized administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The American governmental system "is of such a character as not to admit of clearly defined responsibility for governmental policy on the part of any governmental officer, tends to make difficult the formation of any responsible government at all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to analyze structural obstacles to accountability: separation of powers, checks and balances, decentralized elective offices, and administrative fragmentation that diffuse blame/credit and push responsibility into parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for party-level responsibility when formal government diffuses accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Because responsibility cannot always be fixed in government, "the electors must... look to the party, and within the party customs exist and practices are followed... which are not permitted for an instant in the government, but which are tolerated in the party..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether parties provide mechanisms for accountability and whether internal party customs either facilitate or impede holding leaders responsible (e.g., internal sanctions, leader replacement mechanisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary mechanism for making leaders responsible (English model)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The responsibility of the government, in the English sense of the word, to the Parliament is complete... if Parliament is responsible to the people, the responsibility of the government as a whole to the people is also complete."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence of parliamentary features—collective cabinet responsibility, ability of legislature to force ministers to resign, alignment of executive with legislative majority—that concentrate responsibility and enable popular accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of parliamentary government matters for party/leader role (negative vs positive party function)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some parliamentary systems (e.g., Germany) parties are "negative rather than positive" (criticize or amend government measures) while in others (e.g., England) the leader/party initiates government policy and is subject to parliamentary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare whether parties in a system are primarily initiators and controllers of government (creating accountable leadership) or primarily critics with limited capacity to change leadership; this affects how responsibility is institutionalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalization of a single responsible leader (Prime Minister) as concentration of power plus responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prime Minister is the recognized leader in whom is concentrated "power and responsibility in the hands of one man..." though the office may be "unknown to the law but... a proof and a result of the necessity" for such concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a polity has an acknowledged (even if unwritten) mechanism concentrating both authority and accountability in a chief executive (e.g., PM) that parliament and public can hold to account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means used to secure compliance: corrupt patronage/bribery versus recognized authority and cabinet deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Early bosses (e.g., Walpole) used "intrigue, bribery, and corrupt use of governmental powers;" modern Prime Ministers more often rely on "deliberation with his colleagues at recognized Cabinet meetings" and acknowledged authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the methods leaders use to secure party/legislative compliance: whether they rely on corrupt patronage and bribery (negative) or on institutionalized authority, bargaining, and cabinet practices (less corrupt, more legitimate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural causes of boss development: workload on parties, decentralization, and many elective offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of lack of effective political control in government, "the enormous work thrown on the party by such a system has resulted... in the development within the party of a remarkably strong organization" and shifted political influence to the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structural diagnostics: where government fragmentation and many elective offices require parties to perform governance functions, strong party organizations and bosses are more likely to emerge; assess whether design reduces or amplifies this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of press and patronage in molding opinion and securing control
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin of the modern press "is to be found in the efforts of the various party leaders to sway the voting class in their favor," and patronage/money were historically used to secure parliamentary majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine media influence and patronage resources as instruments by which party leaders can build and maintain control; such channels are evaluative factors when judging legitimacy and the health of popular government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against judging the boss solely by means used; consider political development and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The means which the boss uses "should not exercise too great an influence on our ideas as to the propriety of the existence of the boss... political development has generally been accomplished by making use of the means which were at hand without a too nice discrimination as to their propriety..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises objective study: while condemning immoral methods, analysts should also recognize the role of historical circumstances and weigh effectiveness and institutional outcomes alongside moral judgments.
